overall_structure.value: Local microstructural heterogeneity in M2-IA arises from elemental partitioning during IA: Mn and C partition from α/δ-ferrite into austenite while Si partitions from austenite into both δ-ferrite and α-ferrite, raising austenite stability above the equilibrium-composition expectation.

source.reason: Discussion of Mn/C/Si partitioning and local heterogeneity governing M2-IA austenite stability and grain-size distribution.

unmapped_findings: PSE (product of strength and elongation) for M2-IA is 41 GPa%, compared to 61 GPa% for the Si-free M1-IA; the higher PSE of M1 is attributed to its higher retained austenite fraction and finer grains resulting in slower TRIP (b0006, b0061, b0076, b0083).

The stacking fault energy (SFE) of both steels is below 18 mJ/m^2, a critical value below which the alloys are expected to show a TRIP effect; transformation of austenite to martensite is expected during deformation (b0061).
The retained austenite fraction in M2-IA decreases from 19 % before the tensile test to 3.2 % after fracture, demonstrating the occurrence of the TRIP effect during deformation (b0067, figure_011).

Despite a lower retained austenite fraction, the presence of δ-ferrite in M2 enhances partitioning of Mn and C into austenite at IAT, making austenite more stable; as a result both steels possess a favourable combination of strength and ductility (b0073).

The calculated retained austenite fraction at RT for M2-IA (~11 %, from Ms + Koistinen-Marburger model) is lower than the observed fraction (~19 %); this discrepancy is attributed to local microstructural heterogeneities: preferential segregation of elements (Mn from α-ferrite and δ-ferrite to austenite, Si from austenite to δ-ferrite) and a high fraction of finer grains raising austenite stability above the equilibrium-composition expectation (b0055).

The fraction of finer grains is relatively lower for M2-IA than M1-IA, so the extent of austenite stability would be lower in M2-IA; this explains the relatively smaller difference between observed and calculated austenite fractions for M2-IA compared to M1-IA (b0055).
M2-IA exhibits a ductile dimple-rupture fracture; austenite present absorbs strain energy during deformation by transforming into martensite, forming fine dimples (b0066, figure_010).
